title: Learning to Distrust Correct Answers: The Effect of Deliberate AI-Induced Ambiguity on Conceptual Reasoning in Electrical Engineering Students
content: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly becoming part of engineering students’ learning environments, particularly in quantitative problem solving, explanation generation, and formative feedback. The educational value of these systems, however, depends not only on output accuracy but also on whether learners can evaluate claims that appear authoritative. This paper proposes Deliberate Ambiguity Verification (DAV), an instructional framework in which electrical engineering students compare two AI-generated solutions that are mathematically plausible and professionally presented but differ in a consequential assumption, boundary condition, or physical interpretation. Students must identify the point of divergence, verify each response against an independent engineering principle, justify a decision, and report confidence before and after verification. The framework integrates epistemic vigilance, trust calibration, metacognitive monitoring, cognitive engagement, productive failure, and discipline-specific AI literacy. A randomized four-condition design is proposed for students in circuit analysis, contrasting no-AI problem solving, a single AI answer, a plausible-but-incorrect AI answer, and deliberate ambiguity. Primary outcomes are conceptual reasoning, verification behavior, confidence calibration, and AI-free transfer. The paper argues that the goal should not be generalized distrust of AI, but calibrated skepticism: the capacity to determine when an AI response should be accepted provisionally, when it requires independent verification, and when disciplinary reasoning should override the apparent authority of the system. The framework is intended to provide a testable pathway for studying epistemically responsible human-AI collaboration in engineering education.
